title: Halloween Surprise

jokes.text: Am I interrupting something important? Impossible. I work for the government.
jokes.setup: Diane asks if she's interrupting something important, a polite social nicety
jokes.punchline: Ron deadpans that nothing important is possible because he works for the government — self-deprecating institutional cynicism delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Perfectly on-brand for Ron Swanson — his anti-government libertarian worldview expressed in two words of casual dismissal. The economy is exceptional: the setup question is a social pleasantry, the punchline reframes the entire concept of government work in one sentence. Could only be delivered by this character. Slightly docked for originality since it's a well-worn Ron archetype joke.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Visitor
dialogue.line: Am I interrupting something important?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: No. Nothing at government work could be important.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'Her children are loud.' Immediately followed by 'Kung fu!' and chaos
jokes.setup: Ron describes Diane glowingly — 'sharp, confident, strong woman' — then adds a dry coda about her children
jokes.punchline: 'Her children are loud.' — immediately validated by shrieking kids doing kung fu in his office
jokes.explanation: Classic mockumentary structure: the talking-head sets up a contrast, and the scene immediately confirms/extends it. Ron's flat delivery against the ensuing chaos creates the laugh. The juxtaposition between Ron's admiration for Diane and his withering appraisal of her kids is tonally perfect for his character.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown Visitor
dialogue.line: How are the children doing?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Well, they're girls.

jokes.text: Kung fu! / Here comes trouble!
jokes.setup: Kids burst into Ron's government office
jokes.punchline: They immediately start doing kung fu and announce 'Here comes trouble!' — pure chaotic child energy in Ron Swanson's austere domain
jokes.explanation: Works primarily as a visual contrast — chaotic kid energy in Ron's government office. Not especially original but the contrast with Ron's world is inherently funny. The humor is in the situation more than the writing.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: These children are loud and obnoxious. I don't know how parents do it.

dialogue.speaker: Children
dialogue.line: [loud screaming and noise]

jokes.text: Ron stares into the distance after the girls leave and simply says: 'What the hell just happened?'
jokes.setup: Ron, a confirmed bachelor and anti-sentimentalist, has just been swept up into an enthusiastic trick-or-treat invitation by children
jokes.punchline: His lone reaction shot — bewildered, slightly shattered — encapsulates a man confronting domestic life for the first time
jokes.explanation: Six words that do enormous character work. Ron Swanson — a man who controls every aspect of his environment — has just been completely destabilized by small children. The economy is perfect (10 words could not say more than these 5), and it's deeply character-integrated. The laugh comes from seeing Ron's armor crack without melodrama.

dialogue.line: The chaos of children and social interaction

jokes.text: But no trampoline room, correct? / Correct. Like all houses in the world, there's no trampoline room.
jokes.setup: Leslie is touring a house with a realtor, listing amenities
jokes.punchline: She asks about a 'trampoline room' as if it's a standard feature; the realtor's flat response ('like all houses in the world') shows barely-suppressed exasperation
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Leslie's completely sincere desire for a trampoline room, and the realtor's politely incredulous response that reveals this has probably come up before in the showing. 'Like all houses in the world' is a nice piece of exasperated-straight-man writing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, why isn't there a trampoline room?

dialogue.speaker: Realtor
dialogue.line: Because no house has a trampoline room.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But wouldn't every house be better with a trampoline room?

dialogue.speaker: Realtor
dialogue.line: Yes. Every house would be better with a trampoline room.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: 'He would move into my place, but it's a scary nightmare hoarder nest. His words. And Ann's. And the official report filed by the Health Department.'
jokes.setup: Leslie explains why she's looking at houses — Ben can't move in with her
jokes.punchline: The source of this opinion escalates from boyfriend → best friend → OFFICIAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH REPORT, each step making it funnier and more damning
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation structure: each beat is funnier than the last because the source becomes more official and more damning. The fact that Leslie delivers this completely earnestly — not embarrassed — is key to the character comedy. The Health Department detail is the genuinely surprising third beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben can't move in because my landlord said no.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Also, the city said no.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Also, the state said no.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Also, Ben said no.

jokes.text: Leslie asks Martha to say it again so she can react more dramatically to signing the lease
jokes.setup: Leslie says she wants to lease the house; Martha agrees without fanfare. Leslie says 'Thought it was gonna be more dramatic than that.'
jokes.punchline: She asks Martha to repeat it so she can do a more satisfying whoop — treating a mundane real estate moment like a TV-worthy moment
jokes.explanation: Leslie's need to experience life as a triumphant narrative is well-captured here. The bit is slight but the staging — getting the realtor to redo the moment — is a nice absurdist beat. The humor is in Leslie's total unselfconsciousness about how strange this request is.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, that was it? That was my big moment? I need to do this again.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone back to your positions. Martha, you're going to tell me about the potholes again.

dialogue.speaker: Martha
dialogue.line: I... okay?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And this time, I'm going to react with the gravitas this moment deserves.

dialogue.speaker: Martha
dialogue.line: There are potholes on Ramsett Street.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: *gasps dramatically* A pothole? On Ramsett Street? This changes everything!

jokes.text: Chris introduces himself: 'Chris Traeger, city manager, friend, aspiring life coach and recipient of Dr. Richard Nygard's award for Most Improved Patient for my psychotherapy sessions.'
jokes.setup: Chris addresses the Parks Department with an announcement
jokes.punchline: His self-introduction keeps going — from professional titles to a therapy award that he clearly had to ask his own therapist to create for him
jokes.explanation: Works as character establishment — Chris's performative positivity and his deep reliance on therapy are both encoded here. The escalating title list is the vehicle. Slightly bloated in execution but the therapy award payoff is good.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I got an award from my therapist for being her most improved patient.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's great, Chris.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yeah, I started at a nine out of ten in terms of anxiety, and now I'm down to an eight.

jokes.text: Jerry: 'Wow, that's great, Chris. Congrats.' / Chris: 'Thanks, Jerry. It's just a piece of paper and he only made it for me after I specifically asked for it while crying loudly, but... It sure meant a lot to receive it.'
jokes.setup: Chris has just announced he won a 'Most Improved Patient' award from his therapist
jokes.punchline: He immediately deflates the accomplishment: the therapist made it on request, after Chris asked while 'crying loudly' — and then he sincerely says it meant a lot
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. Chris's fragility is on full display — he commissioned his own award from his therapist, did so while crying, and is completely unashamed. The construction is perfect: acknowledgment → deflation → sincere receipt of the deflated thing. The phrase 'crying loudly' is specific in a way that makes it land harder than just 'crying.' Deeply Chris Traeger-coded and deeply funny.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm hosting a horror movie night at my place. We're watching some real shit.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I already posted about it on Instagram, Twitter, and Snapchat. #DonnasHorrorNight is trending.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Don't be late. And don't touch my snacks, motherfucker.

jokes.text: Death Canoe 4: Murder At Blood Lake — 'Seriously? That's the best one! I hope no one minds if I live tweet this bitch.'
jokes.setup: Chris announces the horror movie for movie night
jokes.punchline: The title 'Death Canoe 4: Murder At Blood Lake' is inherently absurd; Donna's enthusiastic authentication of it as 'the best one' plus her plan to live tweet it adds to the comedy
jokes.explanation: The fictional movie title does a lot of work — 'Death Canoe 4' suggests an absurd franchise and 'Murder At Blood Lake' is deliberately redundant camp horror naming. Donna treating this as prestige cinema and immediately planning to live tweet it is strong character comedy. The whole bit builds a joke out of naming alone.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: My therapist is like a beautiful eagle soaring through the vast sky of my emotional landscape, guiding me with majestic wings of wisdom and compassion. I literally cannot function without our sessions.

jokes.text: Chris: 'I am coming dressed as my greatest fear, because Dr. Richard Nygard feels that I should face my fears instead of running from them. He's very wise. I see him five times a week. He holds my life in his hand like a fragile little bird.'
jokes.setup: Chris explains his Halloween costume choice through a therapeutic lens
jokes.punchline: The escalating devotion to his therapist — wisdom acknowledgment → five times a week → 'holds my life in his hand like a fragile little bird' — reveals the full extent of his dependency
jokes.explanation: 'He holds my life in his hand like a fragile little bird' is a wonderfully overwrought image delivered with total sincerity. The escalation from 'he's wise' to total emotional dependency in three beats is well-structured. This is the season's running thread about Chris's mental health played for maximum comedic mileage.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I couldn't have done this without the hard work of everyone on this team.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Actually, I did most of it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, yes, but Tom's social media strategy was really—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I came up with that. Tom just posted it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And Jerry's data analysis was crucial for—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I analyzed it. Jerry just looked at it and nodded.

jokes.text: April's campaign exit: 'Most of all me, April Ludgate, the real hero. Thank you and you're welcome.' Then immediately bolts.
jokes.setup: Ben is giving credit to the campaign team; April wants to leave and return to Pawnee
jokes.punchline: April aggressively self-credits — 'the real hero' — then exits so fast that Ben remarks 'That's an exit. Gone, but never forgotten. Who was that? I'm just kidding.'
jokes.explanation: April's character is well-served here — she's completely sincere about being 'the real hero' while also being eager to escape. Ben's running commentary on her exit ('Gone, but never forgotten. Who was that?') is a nice coda. The double beat of April's shamelessness followed by Ben's mock-eulogy gives the moment two laughs.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: April, you're an amazing person. You've been an incredible addition to this department. You're smart, you're capable, and you're going to do great things. I'm really going to miss you.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Thank you, Ben. That means a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, who are you again?

jokes.text: Diane on princesses: 'Oh, for the last four years everything has been princesses. Every book, every movie, every backpack. All princesses all the time.' Ron: 'Oh, that sounds fun.' Diane: 'It's a nightmare.'
jokes.setup: Ron notices one of the girls is dressed as a princess
jokes.punchline: Ron's clueless 'Oh, that sounds fun' vs. Diane's exhausted 'It's a nightmare' — the gap between a childless person's romanticized view and a parent's reality
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the juxtaposition — Ron's naive enthusiasm vs. a parent's battle-worn reality. Solid observational comedy about parenthood. Not original as a concept but well-executed in context and serves the Ron-as-fish-out-of-water story.

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: My daughters are obsessed with princesses. They want to be princesses, they want to marry princes, they want to live in castles.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's so great! Every little girl dreams of being a princess.

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: No, they don't. Most little girls dream of being doctors, astronauts, and presidents. My daughters are idiots.

jokes.text: Andy's police observation exercise: 'Tree, leaves, night, sky, hand. Andy's hand.'
jokes.setup: Andy is applying to the police academy and needs to work on observation skills
jokes.punchline: His 'observations' are hilariously basic (tree, leaves, night) and culminate in noticing his own hand — as if he just discovered he has one
jokes.explanation: This is excellently Andy-coded — his application of 'observation skills' is a child's list of obvious things, and then he discovers his own hand. 'Andy's hand' as a self-labeling of his own body part is genuinely surreal in the best way. The beat where April reacts ('Pfft. What else you got?') is the perfect straight-man response. Character-perfect and strange enough to be memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wow, check it out. I'm getting really good at this observation thing. Look at all the details I'm noticing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This hand... it's got five fingers. There's a thumb. And look at all these lines on my palm. I bet that means something.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Whoa, and there's hair on my knuckles. I'm like a detective right now.

jokes.text: April's deadpan reaction to Andy's observation list: 'Pfft. What else you got?'
jokes.setup: Andy has just listed 'Tree, leaves, night, sky, hand. Andy's hand.' as his observation exercise
jokes.punchline: April's dismissive 'Pfft. What else you got?' — both mocking him and somehow playing along
jokes.explanation: April's response is the perfect foil beat — simultaneously mocking and affectionate. The character integration is high because only April would respond to Andy's absurdity with disdain-laced encouragement. This works because it lands on exactly the right note of their relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: We had a situation at the school where a student locked themselves in the bathroom and wouldn't come out. Turns out they were trying to flush a whole rotisserie chicken down the toilet.

jokes.text: Diane's exit due to 'pooping on the soccer field': 'Some idiot kids were caught pooping on the soccer field'
jokes.setup: Diane gets an emergency call and has to leave trick or treating suddenly
jokes.punchline: The emergency is kids pooping on the soccer field — absurdly base and school-administrator-specific
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'pooping on the soccer field' as a vice-principal emergency is well-chosen — it's low-stakes and absurdly mundane for someone who has to leave a family outing. Works well as a plot device joke. Not sophisticated but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: I need to go to the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I... I don't know what you want from me.

jokes.text: Princess Mommy has to go take care of some bad guys.
jokes.setup: Diane addresses her daughters in princess-speak to soften her departure
jokes.punchline: Reframing 'kids pooping on a soccer field' as 'bad guys' Princess Mommy must face — wildly incongruent with the reality
jokes.explanation: The irony of calling poop-emergency kids 'bad guys' for a vice principal playing 'Princess Mommy' is a solid incongruity joke. Brief and functional — doesn't overstay its welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Death Canoe 3: the canoe becomes the hero.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, the canoe becomes the hero?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Yeah. It saves everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's ridiculous.

jokes.text: Ron on bathroom emergency: 'I need to go to the bathroom.' / Ron: 'I-I have no idea what to do about that.'
jokes.setup: Ron is left alone with two small girls trick or treating; one immediately says she needs to go to the bathroom
jokes.punchline: Ron's complete helplessness — a man who can build a house from scratch cannot handle a child needing the bathroom
jokes.explanation: Ron's helplessness in the face of child-rearing basics is the core joke of his subplot and this is a well-chosen crystallization of it. The pause before 'I-I have no idea what to do about that' suggests genuine deer-in-headlights paralysis from a supremely competent man. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't go to Florida. Do you know what's in Florida? Alligators. And pythons. Giant pythons that eat alligators.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Pythons don't eat alligators.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude, they don't.

jokes.text: Death Canoe movie night: 'It's the death canoe. Get your foot out the water, dumb-ass! It's blood lake.'
jokes.setup: The scary movie night is underway
jokes.punchline: Donna is deeply invested in the movie — shouting instructions at the screen as if the character can hear her, using the movie's absurd proper nouns earnestly
jokes.explanation: Donna yelling at the film is a well-worn bit but lands because of the specificity of the movie's mythology ('it's blood lake'). The earnestness of the character within the absurd fictional world is the source of the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm on high alert. I see a suspicious character in a clown costume approaching from the north. This could be a Code 47. Wait, he's just handing out candy. False alarm. Oh, but now there's a vampire lurking by the oak tree. Definitely dangerous. I'm gonna need to confiscate all of his candy for evidence.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Now, I missed the first three Death Canoe films. Why exactly is it a death canoe? Does it tip over easily?' / Donna: 'Read my Twitter feed. I live tweeted the first three this morning in preparation.'
jokes.setup: Tom is confused by the movie's mythology
jokes.punchline: Donna prepared for movie night by live-tweeting all three previous Death Canoe films that same morning — treating a campy horror franchise with the reverence of a serious cinephile
jokes.explanation: The bit of Donna doing prep-work for a B-horror movie series is excellent character comedy — she treats it with the seriousness of an awards show. Tom's sincere question ('does it tip over easily?') as a naive plot inquiry is also funny. And the reveal of 'the fifth one, the canoe's actually the hero' adds a genuinely surprising absurdist beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Just break the other one too.

jokes.text: 'In the fifth one, the canoe's actually the hero. It's a crazy twist.'
jokes.setup: Discussion of the Death Canoe franchise
jokes.punchline: Donna matter-of-factly reveals that by Death Canoe 5, the canoe has become the protagonist — delivered as if this is a natural narrative progression
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff of the Death Canoe running gag and it's the best beat in the sequence. The idea of a canoe becoming a hero by the fifth installment — with Donna calling it 'a crazy twist' with total sincerity — is genuinely inspired absurdism. The economy is excellent: one sentence, maximum comedic commitment to the bit. It also works as a parody of franchise storytelling.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I feel like I'm in the middle of World War II, and nobody's telling me which side I'm on.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Florida? They have sharks in Florida. And swamps. And swamp sharks.'
jokes.setup: Jen tells Ben the candidate is in Florida and wants him to run the campaign there
jokes.punchline: Ben's response to 'Florida' is not about logistics but about swamp sharks — an invented but logical portmanteau worry that reveals his anxiety through comic deflection
jokes.explanation: 'Swamp sharks' is a great invention — it follows naturally from 'sharks' and 'swamps' but the combination is its own absurd thing. Ben's anxiety expressed as a nature-documentary concern is very character-appropriate for a nervous, earnest nerd. The escalation from sharks → swamps → swamp sharks has a clean comedic logic.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, on three. One... two...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: THREE!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, we were just trying to—

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'm having chest pains! Call an ambulance!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is not what we planned.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, stay with us!

jokes.text: Ron's Halloween observation report at the door: '7:34 pm. Man dressed as a nerd. Female dressed as crazy witch. Neither of us is in costume. Case closed. Candy, please.'
jokes.setup: Andy is doing his police observation exercise while trick or treating with the girls
jokes.punchline: Ron performs the police-style narration while trick or treating, then immediately drops it for the transactional goal: candy
jokes.explanation: This builds perfectly on Andy's earlier observation exercise — Ron co-opts the form and then abandons it the instant it's no longer useful. 'Case closed. Candy, please.' is excellent comedic economy: the whole police-procedural game deflated in four words. The observation that 'neither of us is in costume' as Ron and Andy are both just dressed normally is a nice self-aware beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I think I'm having a heart attack!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh my God, somebody call an ambulance!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Jerry, stay with us!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I can't breathe, I can't—

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: *farts loudly*

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, come on, man!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That is disgusting.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Really, Jerry? Really?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: For God's sake.

jokes.text: Ron's solution to the tiara dispute: breaks BOTH tiaras. 'There. Now neither of you has a tiara. Problem solved.'
jokes.setup: Zoey broke Ivy's tiara; now one has a tiara and one doesn't — Ron must mediate
jokes.punchline: Ron solves inequality by destroying the remaining tiara — Solomon-style but without the mercy, delivered as if this is obviously correct
jokes.explanation: This is the best Ron Swanson joke of the episode and one of the better character jokes in the series. His solution — annihilating the good tiara to restore equality by making both children have zero — is simultaneously brutal, logical, and perfectly Ron. The delivery of 'Problem solved' as if no reasonable person could object is the key. It's a parody of cold utilitarian thinking applied to a child's toy dispute. High on all craft dimensions; the character integration is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Your husband had a heart attack.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh no!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Are you saying that Jerry's been having gas this whole time and nobody thought to tell me?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Because I have been planning an entire intervention around his digestive issues.

jokes.text: Death Canoe reaction: 'Oh! Right in his face! / Sorry about your jaw, son.'
jokes.setup: The group is watching Death Canoe 4 and something violent happens on screen
jokes.punchline: The characters react to the on-screen violence with enthusiastic delight, quoting the presumably ridiculous movie dialogue ('Sorry about your jaw, son')
jokes.explanation: Functional continuation of the Death Canoe bit. The joke is mostly carried by the absurdity of the fictional movie dialogue ('Sorry about your jaw, son') rather than any character-specific insight. Works as part of the running gag but isn't a standout beat on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Our health insurance plan considers any body part you were born with a pre-existing condition.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Now I know exactly how FDR felt after Pearl Harbor.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is upset that Ben might have to take a job in Florida instead of moving back to Pawnee
jokes.punchline: She compares her relationship uncertainty to FDR's experience of Pearl Harbor — characteristically grandiose historical self-reference
jokes.explanation: Leslie's habit of placing herself in historical context is a well-established character trait. The specific choice of FDR-at-Pearl-Harbor as an analogy for 'my boyfriend might take a job elsewhere' is well-calibrated absurdity. Solid character comedy, not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We should price this hat at 8 cents.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: 8 cents? April, this hat is priceless. I wore it the day I met you. I wore it when we got married. I wore it when we found out we were having a baby.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You've worn that hat like three times.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Each one was magical. I'm thinking we price it at $50,000.

jokes.text: Ann and Leslie's plan to cheer Leslie up: wait outside the bathroom to scare Tom. Leslie: 'That would cheer me up.'
jokes.setup: Ann tries to cheer up Leslie who is stressed about Ben's potential move
jokes.punchline: The adult solution proposed by these two professionals is to hide and scare their coworker coming out of a bathroom — and Leslie immediately endorses it
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the incongruity of adult professionals resorting to a child's prank as emotional therapy. Leslie's immediate enthusiastic approval ('That would cheer me up') is the character beat that makes it work. Sets up the Jerry heart attack gag.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: My house is apparently booby-trapped.

jokes.text: They scare Jerry instead of Tom — and Jerry appears to be having a heart attack while also passing gas spectacularly
jokes.setup: Ann and Leslie hide to scare Tom; Jerry comes out of the bathroom instead
jokes.punchline: Jerry is scared, appears to be having a heart attack, AND releases a spectacular quantity of gas — multiple simultaneous crises, each worse than the last
jokes.explanation: This is a well-constructed escalating disaster — wrong target + heart attack + extreme gas is three simultaneous escalating crises. The show's history of Jerry suffering comedic indignities gives the heart attack emotional weight that makes it funnier. It's a strong physical comedy set piece even described purely through dialogue reactions.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I've had three major relationship phases: the idealist phase, the realist phase, and the 'oh God, what was I thinking' phase.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom somehow managed to get two phases, both negative.

jokes.text: 'Oh, geez! Did a dinosaur just fart?' / 'Jerry, get a grip.' / 'Sorry, guys.' / 'Ugh! Apology not accepted.' / 'Stop talking, moron.' / 'I wish I could stop smelling.' / 'Dude.' / 'Seriously, Jerry, did you eat farts for lunch?'
jokes.setup: Jerry is having a heart attack while also passing gas; the group is trying to help him but is distracted/disgusted
jokes.punchline: Each new reaction to the gas is both funnier and crueler — the group cannot stop commenting on it even as Jerry may be dying
jokes.explanation: 'Did a dinosaur just fart?' is the strongest individual line — Tom's hyperbole for the severity of the gas. The escalating cruelty of the group's reactions even during a cardiac event is dark and funny. 'Did you eat farts for lunch?' is solid lowbrow escalation. As a sustained sequence it's effective cringe/dark comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry's having a medical emergency! He's having a fart attack!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa—that's not what that means.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, a serious fart attack. Call an ambulance!

jokes.text: Tom at the hospital: 'I've got some magazines and those boring word jumbles you like to do. Is there anything else you need, J? Maybe some Gas-X?' / Jerry: 'Ha ha, Tom.' / Tom: 'Ha ha.'
jokes.setup: Tom visits Jerry in the hospital after his heart attack
jokes.punchline: Tom's bedside manner is performing thoughtfulness (magazines!) before landing a Gas-X joke at a man who just had a cardiac event worsened by flatulence
jokes.explanation: Tom being unable to resist the Gas-X joke in a hospital room is true to his character. Jerry's resigned 'Ha ha, Tom' suggests this is a very familiar dynamic. The 'boring word jumbles you like to do' is a nice character detail — a small dehumanizing observation about Jerry's tastes.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: This case made my entire career. My client was a woman from Florida who discovered her husband was having an affair with her sister.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: So she decided to divorce him. But here's where it gets complicated - the husband had already filed for divorce from the sister.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: Turns out the sister was also married to a third man, who was simultaneously divorcing both of them to marry the original husband's brother.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: And the brother? He'd already run off to the Keys with a manatee he claimed to be emotionally bonded with.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: The court ruled the manatee had more legal standing than three of the five parties involved.

jokes.text: Leslie asks the doctor to medically describe what happened. Doctor: 'He had a mild heart attack.' Leslie: 'Yeah, but he also exhibited excessive flatulence. Is there a term for having a heart attack while releasing so much gas?' Doctor: 'Not really.' Leslie: 'I just want to hear the doctor say that Jerry had a fart attack. Is that too much to ask?'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks for a medical description of Jerry's event
jokes.punchline: Leslie's entire goal is to get an official medical authority to say 'fart attack' — she is willing to create medical terminology for this purpose
jokes.explanation: 'Fart attack' is this episode's most quotable coinage. The structure is excellent: Leslie frames the question in medical language, gets a clinical answer, and then drops the pretense to reveal she just wants to hear a doctor say 'fart attack.' 'Is that too much to ask?' is the perfect capping line. High quotability — this phrase likely entered Parks fandom lexicon.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Why is everything so expensive?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Because it's worth it. I don't do discounts. You know why? Because my brand is premium. When you walk into Rent-A-Swag, you're not just renting clothes, you're renting confidence. And confidence doesn't have a sale price.

jokes.text: Jerry: 'No, that's okay. I'm glad this happened. I mean, I could do without the mess of hospital bills, but no, this was a wakeup call.' / 'Well, they did cause it.' / Jerry: 'Hey.'
jokes.setup: Jerry is being gracious about his friends' visit despite them causing his heart attack
jokes.punchline: Gayle notes they caused it — a gentle factual correction to Jerry's generosity — and Jerry responds with a mild 'Hey' that suggests he agrees but is choosing grace
jokes.explanation: The callback beat where Gayle factually confirms 'they did cause it' while Jerry tries to be magnanimous is a nice character moment. Jerry's 'Hey' — not a denial, just a mild protest — is the right comic beat. The dark irony that the people who caused his heart attack are now claiming concern is well-handled.

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: Ron, I'm waiting for an apology.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: An apology? Diane, you have the best posture of anyone in this office. Your spine is like a sequoia.

jokes.text: Insurance anecdote: 'One time I sprained my wrist and our insurance claimed that having a wrist was a pre-existing condition.'
jokes.setup: Leslie explains the Parks Department health care plan is 'kinda crappy'
jokes.punchline: The specific absurdity of insurance denying a wrist injury because 'having a wrist' is a pre-existing condition — a satirically plausible exaggeration of actual insurance practices
jokes.explanation: This is sharp satirical writing. 'Having a wrist is a pre-existing condition' is an elegant reductio ad absurdum of insurance company logic — it sounds insane but follows the real logic of pre-existing condition denials to its endpoint. It's quotable, original in its specific construction, and economical. One of the better standalone joke lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ron, you need to apologize.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't apologize. It's a sign of weakness.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, it's a sign of being a functional human being.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, and right now you're being a stubborn idiot.

jokes.text: Garage sale hat negotiation: 'Babe, how much should I sell this hat for?' / 'I don't know, eight cents?' / 'Honey, this is the hat I was wearing the first time I ever heard Vitalogy by Pearl Jam.' / 'Oh, $900.' / 'Yeah, that sounds about right.'
jokes.setup: Andy wants to price a hat at a fundraiser garage sale; April suggests eight cents
jokes.punchline: The hat has sentimental value (first hearing Vitalogy); April immediately revises to $900 and they both agree this is correct — satirizing the absurd gap between sentimental and market value
jokes.explanation: The joke structure is clean: low offer → sentimental context → absurdly high counter → mutual agreement. The Vitalogy reference works because it's specific enough to feel real without being parody. April's instantaneous recalibration from 8 cents to $900 is the punchline, and Andy's complete acceptance is the second beat. Their relationship dynamic comes through clearly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Do I hear one hundred? One hundred dollars for Ann Perkins, a woman who has it all. She's got the brains of a surgeon, the abs of a personal trainer, and the heart of... well, another surgeon because she's very smart and very fit.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: One fifty! Going once, going twice... This is a woman who can parallel park in her sleep. A woman whose hair is so shiny and voluminous, it has its own zip code.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Two hundred! Ann Perkins is a gift to mankind. She's a gift to Pawnee. She's a gift to me. Sold!

jokes.text: Ron: 'I am selling this table. I made it.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks Ron what he's selling at the garage sale
jokes.punchline: Ron's entire contribution to a fundraiser is one table — that he made himself — and the pride in 'I made it' as justification for its sale is pure Ron
jokes.explanation: Six words, perfect character encapsulation. Ron's handcrafted table is both his contribution and implicitly his entire material attachment to possessions — he made one thing and he's selling it. The economy is exceptional. The joke's comedy is entirely in what it tells us about Ron without stating it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Do I hear fifty dollars for this beautiful, intelligent, and talented woman? Ann Perkins, everybody! Look at her. She's got the body of a four-year-old boy. I mean that as a compliment. Fifty dollars? Going once... going twice... She's very fresh. Not a lot of mileage on this one. Ann, turn around. See that? Very desirable. Do I hear seventy-five? She's got all her original parts. Well, not all of them. She had her appendix out in 1997. But that's fine, that's fine. It actually makes her lighter, easier to transport.

jokes.text: Ron's tripwire admission: 'If the kids ever wanted to come to my place, I'd have to take a whole week off work just to undo the alarms and tripwires.'
jokes.setup: Ron is discussing his feelings about Diane's children potentially being part of his life
jokes.punchline: His practical concern about having children over is not emotional readiness but the literal physical security infrastructure of his home — alarms AND tripwires, requiring a week's dismantling
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Ron Swanson character comedy. The joke works because it treats a practical concern (child safety) as secondary to an absurd one (the home security apparatus Ron has apparently constructed). 'Alarms and tripwires' plural, requiring 'a whole week' to dismantle, reveals a level of fortress-like domestic preparation that is both funny and completely believable for this character. High on originality, character integration, and earned-vs-cheap.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Studies show that 4 out of 5 dentists recommend having an auction.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's not a real statistic.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I just made it up, but I'm very confident in it.

jokes.text: Ann's relationship personality adoption montage: 'Chris Traeger-- exercise phase. Andy Dwyer-- my grunge phase. Tom Haverford-- my needless shopping phase. Also my credit card debt phase.'
jokes.setup: Leslie pointed out that Ann adopts the personality of whoever she's dating
jokes.punchline: The labels on each box confirm this: Ann fully transformed into each boyfriend's archetype — the phases are specific and recognizable to the audience who knows these characters
jokes.explanation: This joke is highly effective for regular viewers who know all three ex-boyfriends — Chris's fitness obsession, Andy's slacker-rock persona, Tom's conspicuous consumption are all accurately reflected. 'My needless shopping phase. Also my credit card debt phase.' as two separate labels for Tom is the best beat — it implies the boxes had to be subdivided.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: So what are your plans for the date?

dialogue.speaker: Bidder
dialogue.line: Well, I thought we'd start with dinner at a nice restaurant.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That sounds lovely!

dialogue.speaker: Bidder
dialogue.line: Then we'll go back to my place and I'll show her my collection of human teeth.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, what?

dialogue.speaker: Bidder
dialogue.line: After that, we can drive out to the woods at midnight and just sit in the car with the engine running.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Okay, I think we need to stop this date.

dialogue.speaker: Bidder
dialogue.line: But I haven't even told her about my dungeon yet.

jokes.text: Leslie's MC announcement: 'As many of you know, Jerry Gergich, our friend, has suffered a devastating fart attack, and we are here to help.'
jokes.setup: Leslie opens the fundraiser auction
jokes.punchline: She officially uses 'fart attack' in a public announcement — the term she lobbied to get the doctor to say has now become the official descriptor
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'fart attack' works because Leslie has officially adopted the term and is using it in a public, formal announcement. The contrast between the formal fundraiser context and the word 'fart attack' is the joke. Strong callback structure — the earlier scene earns this payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Wait, you're actually doing this? You're really going to auction me off?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Of course! Do I hear one hundred dollars for this beautiful, talented woman? Going once... going twice... SOLD to the handsome gentleman in the front row!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's not how this works.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, I'm a professional auctioneer now. I've watched three YouTube videos.

jokes.text: Perd Hapley book: 'The Thing About Me Is I'm Perd Hapley'
jokes.setup: Leslie is auctioning off special items at the garage sale
jokes.punchline: The book title — 'The Thing About Me Is I'm Perd Hapley' — is a perfect parody of Perd's news-anchor verbal tic (over-explaining obvious things) applied to a book title
jokes.explanation: For Parks fans, this is a perfect payoff on Perd Hapley's character — his habit of stating the obvious with portentous gravity applied to his own memoir title. 'The Thing About Me Is I'm Perd Hapley' is written exactly as he speaks, and is funny entirely as character-specific absurdism. High character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm starting a clothing rental business for teenagers. We rent out designer clothes, high-end sneakers, all that stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We're calling it 'Rent the Runway But Make It Fashion' — no wait, that's taken.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: How about 'Threads for Heads'? 'Drip Flip'? 'The Fit Boutique'?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, we're going with 'Young Jeezy's Closet.'

jokes.text: Kurtzwilder's origin story: 'Mine is the classic Florida success story... bam, just like that, gator eats penis.'
jokes.setup: Kurtzwilder tells the story of how he got into law, building up to what sounds like a standard rags-to-riches narrative
jokes.punchline: The story detours into a grotesque Florida-specific news story — an alligator eating a severed penis — as his first big case
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is well-constructed — 'classic Florida success story' primes us for ambition, law school, hard work. The escalation into 'gator eats penis' as a matter-of-fact pivot is an excellent subversion. The full story (cheating husband, masseuse, severed anatomy, alligator) manages to keep escalating even after the punchline. Ben's 'Excuse me?' as a reaction beat is the ideal response.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, I'm so sorry. We only raised $40,000 instead of the $50,000 we needed.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh, that's okay, Leslie. I'm sure you did your best.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, Jerry, this is bad. This means we can't do the whole project. By next year, you'll be even older. By the time we raise enough money, you'll probably be dead.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And frankly, Jerry, if you die before we finish this, no one's going to care. They're just going to remember you as the guy who fell down the well that one time.

jokes.text: Full Kurtzwilder divorce case details: 'Guy cheats on his wife with Dan Marino's masseuse, one day she cuts his junk off, throws it in the Everglades. Why not? Damn alligator ate it.'
jokes.setup: Continuation of Kurtzwilder's Florida divorce case origin story
jokes.punchline: 'Why not?' as a parenthetical aside justifying throwing genitalia into the Everglades — a phrase that encapsulates Florida as a concept
jokes.explanation: 'Why not?' is the single funniest word choice in this extended joke — a casual shrug at a heinous act that somehow works as Florida shorthand. The Dan Marino's masseuse detail is bizarrely specific in the way that real Florida stories often are. This is the extension of a good punchline that keeps paying off.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, don't worry about those medical bills. You know what? I'm going to help you figure this out.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Really? Oh Leslie, that's so kind of you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah. But let's be honest, your financial future is completely destroyed. I mean, you're 60 years old, you have no savings, and you just racked up $40,000 in medical debt. You're going to die poor and alone, Jerry.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Leslie!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm just being honest! That's what friends do!

jokes.text: Tom live-tweets his conversation with Morris while Morris is trying to have it: 'What are you doing now? I'm talking to you.' / 'I'm live tweeting this dumb-ass conversation.'
jokes.setup: Morris is complaining about Tom's spoiler-filled Death Canoe tweets
jokes.punchline: Tom solves the meta-problem of being criticized for tweeting by tweeting the criticism in real time
jokes.explanation: Tom tweeting the complaint about his tweeting is a nicely self-referential character moment. 'I'm live tweeting this dumb-ass conversation' is highly Tom-coded — he doesn't stop doing the thing, he just redirects it. The meta-layer (tweeting about being criticized for tweeting) gives this a bit more structural cleverness than a simple callback.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Want to come over and watch some TV? I just made a fresh batch of Jell-O.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, no. Your apartment smells like old milk and broken dreams. And your Jell-O tastes like what I imagine a tire fire would taste like if it was jiggly.

jokes.text: Tom's $200 scorpion coat: 'You can't sell clothes at a tag sale for more than they're worth.' / Tom: 'Um, watch me.'
jokes.setup: Tom is selling a used coat for $200 at a garage sale
jokes.punchline: He paid $150 and added a scorpion — therefore $200. His complete confidence in this value-add logic, and 'Watch me' as his response to the reasonable objection
jokes.explanation: The detail that Tom added a scorpion to a used coat to justify the markup is very on-brand for him. 'Watch me' as a two-word dismissal of retail logic is a solid punchline. The scorpion is never explained — it's funnier for it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've decided to give each of the children a gift to make amends.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm giving them each a hunting knife.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, no.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What? They're high-quality blades. German steel.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You cannot give children hunting knives.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because they're children, Ron. They could hurt themselves.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: ...Oh. I see your point.

jokes.text: Ron's apology to Diane: Diane asks if he wants to say anything. Ron says 'You look nice today.' Then, after prompting, admits he broke her daughter's tiara.
jokes.setup: Diane accepts Ron's apology but asks if he wants to say anything to her
jokes.punchline: Ron's instinct for 'saying something' to a woman is a compliment ('You look nice today') rather than any acknowledgment of wrongdoing — his social wiring is completely misaligned
jokes.explanation: Ron reading 'do you want to say anything?' as an invitation to pay a compliment rather than apologize is perfect character comedy. It reveals his relationship inexperience and his default male behavior all at once. The pause before 'You look nice today' implies he genuinely thought this was the correct answer.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I love you ridiculously.

jokes.text: 'Too late. Good-bye.' — Diane walks out after Ron fails to apologize.
jokes.setup: Ron has just offered a compliment instead of an apology.
jokes.punchline: Diane's 'Too late. Good-bye.' — delivered without drama, matter-of-fact, as the window closes.
jokes.explanation: Three words doing a lot of character work. Diane's directness matches Ron's, which is part of why they work as a couple. The moment is also slightly bittersweet — the comedy comes with genuine tension. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, I have something I need to ask you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Not yet. I want to savor this moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, go ahead.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, will you—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Stop, stop, stop! Not yet. I'm not ready. Give me five more minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know what this is about?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Of course I know! And I want to remember every second of it. Okay, now I'm ready.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, will you marry—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No! I changed my mind! One more minute!

jokes.text: Andy: 'Dude, you're totally blowing this.' — Ron: 'I'm not gonna apologize. It wasn't even a real tiara, for God's sake.' — Andy: 'Oh, well, relationship over. Too bad.'
jokes.setup: Diane has left. Ron is being stubborn.
jokes.punchline: Andy's 'Oh, well, relationship over. Too bad.' is an unexpectedly blunt, accurate assessment delivered with complete casualness — Andy cutting through Ron's rationalization.
jokes.explanation: Andy's casual relationship wisdom delivered without any sense of importance is good character work. 'Oh, well, relationship over. Too bad.' sounds like he's describing a snack being out of stock. The lightness of delivery against the gravity of the situation is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Children
dialogue.line: Trick or treat!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Isn't it a little late? Halloween was over a week ago.

jokes.text: Andy's observation analysis of Ron's sadness: 'I've trained extensively in the art of observation. You are sad, and we know why. You didn't sell your table. And it's probably a little too expensive.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April tell Ron he's 'totally blowing' his relationship with Diane; Ron denies being sad
jokes.punchline: Andy, claiming extensive observation training, correctly identifies that Ron is sad — but his diagnosis of the cause is that he didn't sell his table (possibly too expensive), completely missing the emotional reality
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. It operates on three levels simultaneously: (1) callbacks Andy's police observation training in a context where it fails completely, (2) Andy gets one thing right (Ron is sad) through the wrong method, then invents a completely wrong cause (unsold table, possibly overpriced), and (3) the table diagnosis is so specific and so wrong that it becomes its own absurdist non sequitur. The 'and it's probably a little too expensive' addition, delivered with the same authority, is perfectly timed escalation. This couldn't come from anyone but Andy Dwyer and the craft is exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I got some Halloween candy for the office.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh great, what did you get?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, I found some expired protein bars from 2003, a handful of sugar-free gum, and some dental floss.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not candy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's better than candy. It's good for your teeth.

jokes.text: Leslie auctions Ann as a date: 'A wonderful surprise item. An evening with sexy nurse Ann Perkins.' / 'No.' / 'Yes.'
jokes.setup: The fundraiser is falling short of its goal; Leslie has to escalate
jokes.punchline: Leslie's solution is to spontaneously auction off her best friend as a date without asking her — Ann's 'No' and Leslie's immediate 'Yes' establishes the dynamic
jokes.explanation: The No/Yes exchange is a good setup for the extended auction bit. Leslie's complete lack of hesitation in selling Ann as a fundraiser item is character-consistent — her conviction that she's doing good overrides all other considerations.

jokes.text: Leslie's auction patter: 'Just dinner and dancing, nothing sexual. Unless she's into that, but no, she's not. Nothing fresh. Don't even try it. But you never know, right? No! No, she's not into it. Don't try anything, but, you know, give it a shot.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is auctioneering Ann as a date item
jokes.punchline: Leslie's auctioneer patter becomes a contradicting spiral — simultaneously warning bidders off sexual interest while also encouraging it, completely undermining herself in real time
jokes.explanation: The escalating self-contradiction is the joke — Leslie starts with a boundary, immediately softens it, then walks it back, then hedges again. 'Don't try anything, but, you know, give it a shot' is the comedic peak — two completely opposite instructions in one sentence. This is good character comedy about Leslie's inability to follow a simple rule when she's improvising.

jokes.text: 'Three out of four married couples have met each other at spontaneous auctions.' / 'I don't think that's true.' / 'I d--well, I don't know, I--' / '$100.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to justify auctioning Ann by citing dubious statistics
jokes.punchline: Ann correctly calls out that the statistic is made up; Leslie can't defend it and is mid-stammer when the first bid cuts off the argument
jokes.explanation: Leslie inventing a completely fictional statistic ('three out of four married couples') and being caught mid-justification by the first bid is well-timed. The $100 cutting off her half-explanation is the punchline, turning her embarrassment into the auction's opening.

jokes.text: Bidder's date plan: 'My cousin's got a kickass mud pit in his yard. She could watch me do belly flops then we maybe we could get some Thai food and a tank of nitrous and see what happens.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks what the high bidder (tank top, tattoos) would do on his date with Ann
jokes.punchline: The date plan progresses through mud pit belly flops → Thai food → nitrous oxide, presented as a completely normal and romantic evening
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdity of the date plan (mud pit → belly flops → Thai food → NITROUS) maintains a consistent internal logic — this person genuinely thinks this is a good date. 'See what happens' after a tank of nitrous is a great capper. Leslie's reaction ('Oh, that's not as bad as I thought it would be') is the straight-man punchline.

jokes.text: Ann outbids everyone on herself: 'I am going to bid a million dollars on myself. Going once, going never, sold.'
jokes.setup: Ann has been watching the bidding on her escalate to disturbing levels
jokes.punchline: Ann ends it by bidding $1 million on herself and calling the auction — 'going once, going never' subverts the standard auction formula
jokes.explanation: 'Going once, going never, sold' is a smart subversion of auction language — 'going never' as a replace for 'going twice' is the right wordplay. Ann's self-rescue via absurd bid is a good character beat. Economical and well-constructed.

jokes.text: Tom's Rent-a-Swag pitch: 'High end clothes rentals for teens, tweens and everything in betweens. That jacket is 20 bucks a week.'
jokes.setup: A kid wants to buy Tom's overpriced jacket; Tom pivots from selling to renting
jokes.punchline: 'Teens, tweens and everything in betweens' — Tom has invented a rental business on the spot and already has the marketing language ready, including a rhyming tagline
jokes.explanation: Tom Haverford inventing businesses is a core character trait, and the fact that he improvises a full business model with a rhyming tagline on the spot is great. 'Everything in betweens' as a wordplay-inflected demographic definition is clever and Tom-coded. This is also a planted seed for a future storyline, making it a rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: Leslie's devastating hospital speech: 'I'm sorry, Jerry, but your future has been canceled. We only raised $1,200... the inevitable follow-up problems, and the lifetime of chronic misery that awaits you.'
jokes.setup: Leslie comes to deliver fundraising results to Jerry.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's update becomes a comprehensive itemization of Jerry's grim prospects — 'lifetime of chronic misery' — delivered with genuine sympathy and total obliviousness to how devastating her bedside manner is.
jokes.explanation: 'Your future has been canceled' and 'lifetime of chronic misery that awaits you' are wonderfully bleak lines delivered by someone who thinks she's being helpful. Leslie's catastrophizing combined with her genuine care for Jerry creates the comedy — she's devastating while trying to be supportive. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Leslie's catastrophizing in Jerry's hospital room: 'With all your bills, and the inevitable follow-up problems, and the lifetime of chronic misery that awaits you. I mean, you had this whole plan for your retirement and your beach house and now your future is just a huge pile of crap.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is apologizing to Jerry that the fundraiser only raised $1,200
jokes.punchline: Leslie's attempt at support spirals into a full catastrophizing monologue about Jerry's bleak future — completely inverting the purpose of a hospital visit
jokes.explanation: 'Your future is just a huge pile of crap' delivered as a consolation in a hospital room is a perfect Leslie Knope moment — her anxiety and need to fix things turns into a devastatingly unhelpful speech. Character-integrated and escalating well.

jokes.text: Jerry's response to Leslie's catastrophizing: invites her to watch his stories and mentions 'Tonight's strawberry Jell-o night!' / Leslie: 'Oh, my God, your life is so depressing. No thank you.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Jerry his future is a 'huge pile of crap'; Jerry reframes with genuine contentment — Jell-o night and his stories
jokes.punchline: Leslie is MORE distressed by Jerry's humble contentment than by his medical situation — she can't accept that strawberry Jell-o night is genuinely sufficient for him
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully constructed joke about the contrast between Leslie's ambition and Jerry's genuine happiness. The subversion is that Jerry is actually fine — content, philosophical, excited about Jell-o — and Leslie's 'Oh, my God, your life is so depressing' is the joke: she's projecting. 'No thank you' as an exit line is perfect. The joke also works as a genuine character insight.

jokes.text: Jen: 'Yeah, yeah, I get it. Feelings and girlfriend and whatever. The point is just yesterday you said to me, I'm never happier than when I'm managing a campaign. I don't think I said that. You didn't have to. I watched you in Florida. You were saying it with your heart.'
jokes.setup: Ben is wrestling with the Florida job offer and his relationship with Leslie
jokes.punchline: 'Feelings and girlfriend and whatever' as Jen's dismissal of everything emotional; then her absurd quasi-psychic claim that she knew what he was saying 'with his heart'
jokes.explanation: 'Feelings and girlfriend and whatever' is a great Jen Barkley line — she's a character who operates entirely in outcomes, and emotions are just noise. The pivot to 'you were saying it with your heart' as something she claims to have observed is funny because it's the opposite of her normal mode — coldly reading subtext.

jokes.text: Ron's apology gift: flowers, chocolates, and grout cleaner. 'I noticed you needed grout cleaner, so I brought that too.' / Diane: 'Very romantic.'
jokes.setup: Ron comes to apologize to Diane and has brought gifts
jokes.punchline: The gifts escalate from romantic (flowers, chocolates) to completely utilitarian (grout cleaner) — Ron cannot sustain the romantic gesture without lapsing into practical problem-solving
jokes.explanation: The grout cleaner is an outstanding detail — it's exactly what Ron Swanson would do, noticing a practical need and addressing it even in the middle of a romantic gesture. 'I noticed you needed grout cleaner, so I brought that too' delivered without embarrassment is the character perfectly expressed. Diane's dry 'Very romantic' is the ideal straight-man response. High character integration, and the escalation from romantic to utilitarian is textbook.

jokes.text: 'I did bring the girls something.' [pause] 'I thought I could teach 'em to saw.' [pause] 'I now realize that seems dangerous.'
jokes.setup: Ron is winning Diane back; he says he brought the girls something
jokes.punchline: The gift for two small children is sawing lessons. Ron's immediate self-correction ('I now realize that seems dangerous') suggests he genuinely didn't anticipate this objection
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode. 'I thought I could teach 'em to saw' is a perfect Ron Swanson gift — woodworking as an expression of love, completely divorced from the recipients' age or safety. The self-correction 'I now realize that seems dangerous' is what elevates it: Ron is having this realization in real time, which means he genuinely hadn't thought about it before. The beats (gift reveal → pause → self-correction) are ideally spaced. It's also a deeply sweet gesture in Ron's idiom — he's offering what he loves. High on all craft dimensions. Comparable in quality to classic Ron Swanson moments.

jokes.text: Leslie keeps stopping Ben's proposal to 'remember every little thing about how perfect my life is right now'
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to propose to Leslie at the house she was going to lease; she asks him to wait — twice
jokes.punchline: Leslie pauses the proposal multiple times to savor the pre-proposal moment, making Ben hold the ring while she emotes — her need to experience and archive every moment extends even to proposals
jokes.explanation: Leslie stopping a marriage proposal to properly memorize the moment before it happens is peak Leslie Knope. The absurdity of making Ben pause mid-knee is funny; the sincerity of her reason is also sweet. The double interruption escalates the bit. High character integration — only Leslie would do this.

jokes.text: Leslie says 'Yes!' before Ben finishes the question 'Leslie Knope, will you--' / She says yes; he continues '...marry me?' / 'Oh, yeah.'
jokes.setup: Ben begins his proposal; Leslie has been holding herself back from responding
jokes.punchline: She answers before he can finish the question — her 'Oh, yeah' after he adds 'marry me?' implies she would have said yes regardless of what the question was
jokes.explanation: 'Oh, yeah.' as Leslie's response to the actual word 'marry me?' — after already saying yes — is perfectly calibrated. The implication that she would have accepted any question is deeply Leslie. The joke is embedded in what should be a purely emotional scene, and it works without undercutting the sentiment.

jokes.text: Trick or treaters at the door after the proposal: 'Trick or treat!' / 'It's November 8th.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Andy have brought Diane's daughters to trick or treat at a random house after Halloween has passed
jokes.punchline: The homeowner points out it is November 8th — it has been a week since Halloween — and yet they are there, in costume, demanding candy
jokes.explanation: 'It's November 8th' lands because the number is specific — not just 'it's past Halloween' but a precise date, implying exactly how much time has passed. Ron's complete unfazedness at this objection is implied. A clean closing tag joke.

jokes.text: Ron's explanation at the door: 'Yes, well, these girls didn't get a chance to go trick or treating so somewhere in this house there is some candy. Why don't you find it and we'll get right out of your hair.'
jokes.setup: The homeowner notes it's November 8th; Ron explains without apology or embarrassment
jokes.punchline: Ron instructs a stranger to go find candy in their own house for these children as if this is a completely normal request — 'we'll get right out of your hair' implies they are doing the homeowner a favor
jokes.explanation: Ron's complete self-assurance in this entirely unreasonable request is the joke. 'Somewhere in this house there is some candy. Why don't you find it' is delivered as if Ron is helping the homeowner organize their pantry. 'We'll get right out of your hair' — as if they're the inconvenienced party — is the perfect closer. Excellent character integration and economy.

jokes.text: The homeowner produces calcium chews and a roll of cookie dough as 'candy'
jokes.setup: The homeowner scrambles to find candy on November 8th
jokes.punchline: The best they can do is calcium chews and raw cookie dough — not real Halloween candy, but Ron accepts it as 'tremendous'
jokes.explanation: The calcium chews as 'candy' is a good visual gag payoff — the girls being grateful for what is essentially a nutritional supplement and raw dough is charming and funny. Ron's 'Tremendous. Appreciate it.' delivered with complete sincerity rounds off the episode's subplot on a perfect note.

tmdb_overview: A new job offer for Ben causes Leslie to contemplates their future. Meanwhile, Ron and Andy take Diane's girls out trick-or-treating, and Tom searches for a new business idea.
insight: Halloween-themed episode underperforms with 72.4 score despite character comedy strength.
